extracted.intended_audience: physicians, public-health workers, educators, engineers, and informed general public
extracted.subtask_description: Extract and summarize the evaluative criteria and prescriptive recommendations embedded in Popular Science Monthly essays on education/health, bactericidal disinfection, and heat-engine theory. Focuses on practical tests, recommended practices, and theoretical standards cited in the articles.

rubrics_metrics.name: Education as conserver of psychical and physical health
rubrics_metrics.description: How far education may act as a conserver of psychical, and secondarily of physical health is a legitimate object of inquiry.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Education should aim to preserve mental equilibrium and thereby protect physical health; proper training can reduce predisposition to neuropathic complaints and hysteria by building nerve-strength and self-control.

rubrics_metrics.name: Employ a girl's faculties equally
rubrics_metrics.description: It is the first business of the teacher to employ a girl's faculties as equally as possible—to restrain those which unduly predominate, and exercise the weaker powers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Curricula and classroom practice should deliberately strengthen underdeveloped mental faculties rather than only exercising dominant/emotional tendencies; balance intellectual training to reduce emotional over-dominance that may harm health.

rubrics_metrics.name: Education should cultivate control of mind, not superficial facts
rubrics_metrics.description: The radical defect in the education of girls is that knowledge, and that of a very superficial sort, instead of the cultivation of the faculties, is made its aim.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Teach students that school is for developing control of attention and thought (analogous to scales/exercises in music) rather than memorizing facts to 'appear educated'; emphasize habits of sustained, directed intellectual activity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Train willpower as primary objective
rubrics_metrics.description: Her will-power, the force which will, more than any other, make or mar her, should receive the most careful training.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design exercises and responsibilities that build determination and the ability to turn attention away from damaging emotions or habits; treat will-training as central to preventing nervous breakdowns.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid premature end of childhood
rubrics_metrics.description: The first mistake in the education of girls ... is made when they are allowed to leave childhood too soon. To keep them little girls as long as possible ... is the first step in the right direction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Delay adult responsibilities and social pressures that force early maturity; preserve age-appropriate play and lower pressure during developmental years to protect physical and mental health.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid indoor study for anemic or developing girls
rubrics_metrics.description: Permitting growing girls to sit in the house and study when their transparent cheeks tell of anaemia and lowered vitality is inexcusable; branches of knowledge that are excellent training should be pursued out of doors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer outdoor study, physical activity, and sunlight for adolescents showing low vitality; schedule studies and school routines with physiological needs in mind (fresh air, exercise, sensible hours).

rubrics_metrics.name: Make school-life preparatory, not final
rubrics_metrics.description: The third mistake is making the school-life of girls final, when it ought to be a simple preparation for the intellectual life of the adult woman.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design schooling to cultivate lifelong intellectual habits and the capacity for ongoing study, not merely to produce a transient 'educated appearance' at school-leaving.

rubrics_metrics.name: Teach women laws of their physical and mental life
rubrics_metrics.description: Withholding a knowledge of the laws to which woman is subject, in her physical and her mental life, her place in nature, and the potential character of her mental states and habits is a mistake.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide instruction on physiology, mental hygiene, and the likely effects of emotional states so women can anticipate and manage health risks.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prevention and mental treatment for hysteria and neuropathic complaints
rubrics_metrics.description: For the cure of hysteria and allied complaints physicians declare that skillful mental treatment is better than all the drugs in the pharmacopoeia ... But better than any remedy is prevention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Emphasize preventive physical, mental, and moral training; in treatment prefer psychical/mental therapeutic approaches (sympathy, mental discipline) where causes are nervous rather than relying solely on drugs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unfailing test of bacterial death: reproductive capacity
rubrics_metrics.description: The only unfailing test is afforded by the reproductive faculty: when reproduction ceases, and cannot be excited, the organisms may be considered dead.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In bacteriology and disinfection studies, assess viability by attempting to culture/recover reproduction rather than relying on appearance or temporary inactivity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practical disinfection should destroy spores' vitality
rubrics_metrics.description: The practical object of disinfection should be to go beyond securing a suspension of animation of the bacteria, and to seek to destroy the vitality of the spores.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Disinfection protocols must aim to kill both vegetative bacteria and resistant spores; methods that merely inactivate organisms temporarily are inadequate for true disinfection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limitations of dry heat and importance of moist heat
rubrics_metrics.description: They are generally more easily destroyed by heat when moist than when dry, but even a boiling heat will not destroy some of them when they are in fluids of a neutral reaction ... The degree of heat required to destroy the germs of infectious diseases is believed to be greater than it is practicable to apply by the dry process to clothing and similar materials.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer moist-heat sterilization (e.g., autoclaving) for reliable killing of bacteria and spores; recognize that dry-heat processes may require impractically high temperatures/times and may leave spores viable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Aseptic test for candidate bactericidal substances
rubrics_metrics.description: That active bacteria, when transplanted into a supporting mixture to which a substance supposed to be poisonous to them has been added, should cease to propagate themselves and die out. This may be called the aseptic test.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate antiseptic/aseptic claims by transplant experiments: introduce organisms into growth medium containing the test substance and verify cessation of propagation (culture-based assessment).

rubrics_metrics.name: Antiseptic test for bactericidal efficacy
rubrics_metrics.description: That, when the supposed poison is introduced into a solution swarming with bacteria, all living examples should be killed. This may be called the antiseptic test.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Introduce the substance into heavily contaminated solutions and verify complete killing of viable organisms by culture; distinguish antiseptic (kills existing organisms) from aseptic (prevents propagation of transplanted organisms).

rubrics_metrics.name: Preventive test for candidate disinfectants
rubrics_metrics.description: That substances favorable to the development of bacteria should remain free from them when the substance to be tested is added to them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Add candidate substance to media that normally support bacterial growth and confirm that decomposition/growth is prevented as an indication of preventive (prophylactic) action.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ranking and effective concentrations of aromatic products (preventives)
rubrics_metrics.description: Various aromatic substances, the products of fermentation, were added ... They proved efficacious in preventing, suspending, or wholly stopping decomposition in the following order, according to the strength: As Preventives of Decomposition: Indol in a proportion of 1:1,000; Kresol 2:1,000; Phenylacetic acid 2.5:1,000; Carbolic acid 5:1,000.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When assessing aromatic disinfectants as preventives, use the listed relative potencies and proportions as experimental reference points; note solubility limitations for some compounds.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ranking and concentrations for aseptic (poisoning supporting fluid)
rubrics_metrics.description: As Aseptics — killing transplanted organisms by poisoning the supporting fluid: (text lists scatol, hydrocinnamic acid, indol, kresol, phenylacetic acid, carbolic acid with indicated small proportions).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the small concentration ranges identified (fractions per 1,000) as starting points to test a compound's ability to prevent propagation of transplanted organisms; interpret numbers cautiously (original text gives approximate proportions such as scandol ~0.4–0.8:1000 for some entries).

rubrics_metrics.name: Concentrations and time for antiseptic (killing) action
rubrics_metrics.description: As Antiseptics — wholly destroying all living bacteria: Scatol 0.5:1,000 in 24 hours; Hydrocinnamic acid 0.8:1,000 in 24 hours; Phenylacetic acid in saturated solution (1:400) immediately; Indol saturated (1:900) in 24 hours; Kresol 5:1,000 in 24 hours; Carbolic acid 20:1,000 immediately.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess bactericidal (antiseptic) performance by both concentration and contact time; some agents require much higher concentrations or longer exposure to achieve total kill — carbolic acid and some phenyl compounds may act rapidly at higher concentrations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Substances and chemicals fatal to bacteria
rubrics_metrics.description: The substances which are fatal to the life of the bacteria: concentrated mineral acids, iodine, bromine, chlorine, the sulphates of copper and zinc, corrosive sublimate, benzoic acid and its salts, salicylic and metasalicylic acids, quinia, many aromatic substances, and alcohol; carbolic acid is high in repute.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use these classes of chemicals (acids, halogens, heavy-metal salts, phenolics, alcohols) as known bactericidal agents; selection should consider material compatibility, solubility, toxicity, and effectiveness against spores.

rubrics_metrics.name: Bacterial nutritional/support requirements and their disinfection implications
rubrics_metrics.description: No increase of bacteria takes place without the presence of a suitable substance to support them. The most favorable non-nitrogenous substance is sugar; among nitrogeneous substances the most favorable are the albuminoids; among mineral matters potash, phosphorus, magnesia, and sulphur.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Controlling or removing nutrient/supporting substances (e.g., reducing available proteins, sugars, minerals) or altering their availability (dilution, desiccation) can halt growth transiently but may not kill spores; sanitation should include removing nutrient substrates as a complement to chemical/thermal methods.

rubrics_metrics.name: Effects of desiccation, dilution, light, electricity, and oxygen
rubrics_metrics.description: Taking away water suspends development but restoration restarts it. Privation of light has no effect. The operation of electricity has not been enough observed. Oxygen greatly speeds development but it can take place without it; bacteria are not developed in nitrogen, hydrogen, carbonic oxide, carbonic acid, nitrous oxide, and illuminating gas.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design disinfection/storage strategies with these environmental effects in mind: desiccation/drying can suspend activity (but not sterilize spores), dilution can suppress decomposition, light is not reliably bactericidal per se, and oxygen availability modulates growth rate but is not an absolute requirement for many species.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dry disinfection practical-testing protocol
rubrics_metrics.description: To test the value of the dry process as applied to infected clothing, pieces were impregnated with bacteria-bearing fluids, dried slowly, kept long, then exposed for five minutes to 125°–150° C (or one to two minutes to a higher temperature) and thereafter produced no perturbation when placed into suitable fluid.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate dry-heat disinfection by impregnating representative materials, applying controlled thermal exposures (noted temperature/time regimes), and assessing recovery by reintroduction into growth media; note that while organisms may be killed, spores can remain viable unless higher or longer treatments are used.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reversible engine as theoretical perfect motor (thermodynamic standard)
rubrics_metrics.description: A reversible heat-engine ... running forward and performing a certain amount of work by means of a given amount of heat derived from a source, would, if run backward by the performance upon it of the same amount of work, restore to the source the same amount of heat.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the reversible-engine ideal as the theoretical yardstick for maximum possible efficiency; compare real engine cycles to the reversible limit (Carnot ideal) to evaluate irreversibilities and unavoidable waste.

rubrics_metrics.name: Two physical axioms that bound heat-engine performance
rubrics_metrics.description: The proof rests upon two assumptions ... 1. That a perpetual motion is impossible; 2. That it is impossible by means of inanimate material agency to derive mechanical effect from any portion of matter by cooling it below the temperature of surrounding objects.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When assessing claims about engine performance or novel thermodynamic devices, reject proposals that violate these axioms (perpetual motion or extracting work by cooling below ambient via inanimate means); use them to judge plausibility of efficiency improvements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inevitable waste-heat in heat-to-work conversion under planetary conditions
rubrics_metrics.description: Heat cannot be transformed into mechanical effect without wasting a considerable portion of the energy due to it ... a portion of that heat must ... pass through the engine and raise the temperature of other bodies to no useful purpose.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Accept that practical heat-engines will necessarily reject some heat to a sink; evaluate engines by how closely they approach the theoretical (reversible) efficiency and by the magnitude of unavoidable waste heat rather than expecting perfect conversion.
